pages.intro: People search for a depression quiz when something has gone flat and they want a name for it. Theraglee's low-mood check-ins will not give you a diagnosis, because a quiz cannot honestly give anyone one. What they can do is help you see the shape of a low patch: how long it has been going on, what it is touching, and what tends to lift it even slightly.

You do not have to be in crisis to deserve one.

pages.title: CBT Thought Record Worksheet — Theraglee
pages.description: A printable CBT thought record worksheet, plus a plain-English walkthrough of each column and a worked example. Catch the thought, check the evidence, write a fairer version.
pages.intro: A thought record is the most-used worksheet in cognitive behavioral therapy, and it is not complicated: you catch a thought that made you feel worse, write down what was actually happening, and check the thought against the evidence instead of against your mood. Doing it on paper matters. Thoughts that feel airtight in your head tend to get looser once they have to sit still in a column.

blocks.h2: The seven columns, in plain English
blocks.html:
1. Situation. Where you were and what happened, in one line. Facts a camera could have caught, not interpretations.
  2. Mood. One or two words, and a number out of 100 for how strong it was.
  3. Automatic thought. The sentence that went through your head. Write it exactly, including the harsh version.
  4. Evidence for it. What genuinely supports that thought.
  5. Evidence against it. What does not fit. This column is usually the hardest and the most useful.
  6. A fairer thought. Not a cheerful one. One that accounts for both columns above.
  7. Mood again. The same words, a new number. Even a drop of ten points counts.

Situation: Sent a message to a friend at 9am. No reply by 6pm.
Mood: Anxious, 75.
Automatic thought: "She is annoyed with me and I have ruined it."
Evidence for: She usually answers the same day. Our last call felt a bit short.
Evidence against: She told me last week that work is brutal until Friday. She has gone quiet for two days before and it meant nothing. Nothing in my message was unkind.
A fairer thought: "The silence probably belongs to her week, not to me. If it is still quiet on Saturday I will ask."
Mood again: Anxious, 40.

Fill one in close to the moment if you can, because the thought is easier to catch while it is still warm. Aim for a handful over a week rather than one perfect one. The point is not any single record; it is that after a dozen you start recognizing your own repeat offenders while they are happening.

The Theraglee version is fillable online and saves to your dashboard, so the record builds up over time: open the Thought Record Worksheet.

blocks.h2: If you are working with a therapist
blocks.html: Bring the records. A therapist reading four of your real thought records learns more about the pattern in five minutes than they could from a long description of it. If you do not have a therapist yet, our guide on how to find a therapist covers where to start.

pages.title: 12 Journal Prompts for Burnout — Theraglee
pages.description: Twelve journal prompts for burnout, written for the flat and depleted kind of week rather than the busy kind. Free to read, with a burnout check-in and related worksheets.
pages.intro: Most journal prompts assume you have energy to reflect. Burnout is the condition of not having that, which is why the usual gratitude questions land so badly when you are in it. These twelve are written for the flat weeks: short, concrete, and answerable in three lines when three lines is all you have.

blocks.html:
1. What did today cost you that yesterday did not?
  2. Name the last time you felt genuinely rested. Not asleep. Rested.
  3. Which part of your week are you already dreading, and when did it start being like that?
  4. If someone described your month back to you without using the word "busy", what word would they use?

1. What are you doing out of habit that nobody would notice if you stopped?
  2. Which task takes ten minutes and which one only feels like it does? Write both down and compare.
  3. Who gets your best attention right now, and who is getting what is left?
  4. What have you said yes to this month that you would say no to if asked today?

1. What is one thing that still works — small, unglamorous, reliable?
  2. When did you last do something badly and it was fine?
  3. What would the next two weeks look like if you were allowed to do the minimum?
  4. What is the first thing you would put down, if you were told you had to put one thing down?

blocks.h2: How to use them without making it another task
blocks.html:
Pick one. Not four. Set a timer for five minutes and stop when it goes, even mid-sentence, especially mid-sentence. Burnout gets worse when recovery turns into another thing you are failing at, so an unfinished answer is a finished session.

The Theraglee journal keeps your entries private to your account and gives you a fresh prompt whenever you want one.

blocks.h2: Is it burnout or is it something else
blocks.html: Burnout, ordinary stress, and a low mood all feel similar from the inside and want different things from you. Stress or Burnout: How to Tell the Difference is free to read and lays out where the line usually sits. If it has gone on for months, or if it has followed you into the parts of your life that are supposed to be the rest, that is worth taking to a therapist.

pages.title: How to Find a Therapist: A Step-by-Step Guide — Theraglee
pages.description: What the license letters mean, how much therapy costs, where to look, what to ask on a first call, and what to do when nobody has openings. A practical US guide.
pages.intro: Finding a therapist is mostly an administrative problem wearing an emotional one's clothes. The hard part is rarely deciding you want help; it is the directories, the voicemail, the insurance page that does not load, and the ten people who are not taking clients. Here is the whole process, in the order you will actually hit it.

blocks.html:
In the United States you will mostly meet four kinds of clinician. Any of them can do good talk therapy, and the letters matter less than the fit.

  • LPC / LPCC / LMHC — licensed professional or mental health counselor. Master's level, trained specifically in counseling.
  • LCSW / LICSW — licensed clinical social worker. Master's level, often the strongest on the practical scaffolding around a life, not only what is inside it.
  • LMFT — licensed marriage and family therapist. Trained to treat the relationship or the family as the thing in the room, not only the individual.
  • PsyD / PhD psychologist — doctoral level, and the ones who can do formal psychological testing.

A psychiatrist (MD or DO) is a different job: they prescribe and manage medication, and many do not do weekly talk therapy at all. Plenty of people see both.

blocks.h2: 2. Decide in person, video, or either
blocks.html:
Deciding this first cuts the search down enormously. Video opens up your whole state instead of your neighborhood, and it is the difference between a session and no session on a week with no childcare. In person is worth the travel for some people and some kinds of work. Either is a perfectly good answer, and saying so widens your options rather than narrowing them.

One rule that surprises people: your therapist generally has to be licensed in the state where you are sitting during the session, not where they are.

Out of pocket, a private-practice session in most of the United States runs roughly 100 to 250 dollars, higher in expensive metros and for doctoral-level clinicians. Three things bring that down, and all three are worth asking about directly:

  • In-network. You pay a copay. Call the number on your insurance card and ask for in-network outpatient mental health providers taking new patients.
  • Out-of-network reimbursement. You pay in full, the therapist gives you a superbill, and your plan pays part of it back. Ask your plan what percentage, and whether the deductible applies.
  • Sliding scale. Many therapists hold a few reduced-fee slots. You have to ask; almost nobody advertises them.

Work more than one channel at once, because response rates are low everywhere.

  • Your insurer's provider directory, for the copay path.
  • A public directory of licensed clinicians, like the Theraglee directory, where every listing is license-verified against a state board before it goes live.
  • Your doctor, who often keeps a short list of people they actually refer to.
  • If you are employed, your EAP. It is usually a handful of free sessions and a fast way in.
  • Community mental health centers and university training clinics, which are the most reliable low-cost options and are routinely overlooked.

blocks.h2: 5. Let them come to you instead
blocks.html: The part people find hardest is the cold outreach: leaving voicemails and waiting. Theraglee Match Mode turns that around. You flip a switch on your dashboard and verified therapists in your area can see a pseudonymous profile — your age range, the broad topics you want to work on, whether you prefer in-person, video, or either, your insurance plan, and the first three digits of your zip code so they know you are nearby. They message your Theraglee inbox. Your name stays private unless you choose to reply, and you can block any therapist with one tap. It is free with any account. Create a free account to switch it on.

blocks.h2: 6. What to ask on the first call
blocks.html:
Most first contacts are a free ten or fifteen minute call. Five questions get you most of the way:

  1. Have you worked with people bringing what I am bringing?
  2. What does a typical session with you look like?
  3. What do you charge, and do you have any sliding-scale slots?
  4. What is your availability, and how far out is your waitlist?
  5. How do you handle it if this turns out not to be a fit?

You are also listening to something the answers do not contain: whether you can imagine talking to this person on a bad day.

blocks.h2: 7. Giving it a fair trial, and changing your mind
blocks.html: Three or four sessions is the usual guidance before judging a fit, because the first one is largely history-taking and almost nobody feels a click in it. That said, if you dread going, or feel judged, or find yourself managing their feelings instead of yours, that is information and it arrives early. Leaving a therapist is a normal professional event, not a betrayal. "I do not think this is the right fit, thank you" is a complete sentence, and a good therapist will often hand you two names on the way out.

This is common and it is not a sign you are searching wrong. Ask to be put on waitlists — plural, and say yes to all of them. Ask each person you speak to for two names, since clinicians know who has space. Widen to video across your whole state. Try the training clinics. And if you are getting worse while you wait, call or text 988 in the United States for the Suicide and Crisis Lifeline, or text HOME to 741741. Waiting for an opening is not the same as having no options tonight.

faq.q: How much does therapy cost in the United States?
faq.a: Roughly 100 to 250 dollars a session out of pocket in most of the country, more in expensive metros. In-network insurance reduces it to a copay, out-of-network plans often reimburse part of it, and many therapists keep a few sliding-scale slots that are not advertised.

faq.q: What is the difference between an LCSW, an LPC and an LMFT?
faq.a: All three are master's-level licensed therapists who can do talk therapy. Social workers (LCSW) are often strongest on the practical scaffolding around a life, counselors (LPC) are trained specifically in counseling, and marriage and family therapists (LMFT) are trained to work with the relationship or family as a unit.

faq.q: Does my therapist have to be licensed in my state?
faq.a: Generally yes, in the state where you are physically sitting during the session, not where the therapist is.

faq.q: How many sessions before I know if a therapist is right for me?
faq.a: Three or four. The first is mostly history-taking. That said, dreading the sessions or feeling judged is useful information much earlier than that.

faq.q: What if no therapist has any openings?
faq.a: Join several waitlists at once, ask everyone you speak to for two more names, widen the search to video across your whole state, and try university training clinics and community mental health centers.

pages.title: Feelings Wheel: Find the Right Word for an Emotion — Theraglee
pages.description: What a feelings wheel is, how to use one in two minutes, and a full list of emotion words by family. Then try Theraglee's free wheel tools, no account needed.
pages.h1: Feelings wheel: find the exact word for what you are feeling
pages.intro: A feelings wheel is a chart that starts with a handful of broad emotions in the middle and fans out to more specific words at the edge. You find the nearest broad word, then move outward until one of the specific words lands. It takes about two minutes, and it works because "stressed" and "disappointed" and "humiliated" ask for very different things from you.

blocks.h2: The two wheels people usually mean
blocks.html:
Two charts share the name, and they are built on different ideas.

Plutchik's wheel of emotions. Psychologist Robert Plutchik published this one in 1980. It has eight primary emotions arranged like petals: joy, trust, fear, surprise, sadness, disgust, anger and anticipation. Each petal sits opposite its counterpart (joy across from sadness, fear across from anger), gets more intense toward the center and milder toward the edge, and neighboring petals blend into a named mixture, so joy next to trust gives you love. It is a theory of how emotions relate as much as a list of words.

The Feeling Wheel. Therapist Gloria Willcox published this three-ring wheel in 1982 in the Transactional Analysis Journal. Six broad feelings sit in the center: mad, sad, scared, joyful, powerful and peaceful. Each opens onto a middle ring of more specific words, and each of those onto an outer ring of still more precise ones, so "scared" leads to "anxious" leads to "overwhelmed." It was made as a practical tool rather than a theory, and most of the colorful wheels online are descendants of it. Theraglee's own wheel tools follow the same pattern: broad word first, then narrower, then narrower again.

blocks.h2: How to use a feelings wheel in two minutes
blocks.html:
1. Pause on the feeling, not the story. Before you explain what happened, notice what your body is doing: a tight jaw, a sunk chest, buzzing hands.
  2. Pick the nearest broad word. Start in the center. Angry, sad, scared, glad, or something quieter like calm. It only has to be the closest.
  3. Move one ring out. Read the words that branch from it and pick the best fit. "Sad" might become "lonely" or "disappointed" or "guilty," and those are not the same feeling.
  4. Move out once more if you can. The outer ring is where the useful words live. "Lonely" might become "isolated" or "abandoned."
  5. Say the sentence. "I feel ___." Notice whether anything shifts when the word is right. Often the body loosens a little.
  6. Ask what that feeling tends to want. Disappointment wants to be acknowledged. Resentment wants a boundary. Loneliness wants contact. The precise word points at the next step.

If two words both fit, keep both. "Relieved and guilty" is more honest than either alone.

blocks.h2: Why naming an emotion precisely helps
blocks.html:
A vague feeling is hard to do anything with. "I feel bad" does not tell you whether to rest, apologize, speak up or leave. A specific word does. Being able to tell "irritated" from "hurt" from "anxious" is sometimes called emotional granularity, and people who practice it tend to find feelings easier to sit with, because each one comes with a clearer sense of what it is about.

Naming also puts a small gap between you and the feeling. "I am furious" and "I notice I feel furious" describe the same moment, but the second leaves you room to choose what to do next. And the right word is easier to say to another person, which is often where a feeling finally eases. You do not need to feel calm to do this; the wheel is most useful when the feeling is loud and the words are not there yet.

A plain list you can use without any chart. Start with the family, then look for the word that fits.

  • Joy: content, cheerful, grateful, proud, hopeful, playful, excited, delighted, relieved, tender, amused, satisfied.
  • Sadness: disappointed, lonely, hurt, grieving, discouraged, guilty, ashamed, empty, heavy, homesick, regretful, hopeless.
  • Anger: irritated, frustrated, resentful, annoyed, bitter, jealous, indignant, furious, betrayed, provoked, defensive, exasperated.
  • Fear: anxious, nervous, worried, insecure, overwhelmed, helpless, dread, panicky, rejected, inadequate, frozen, exposed.
  • Surprise: startled, confused, amazed, stunned, disoriented, shocked, awed, perplexed, dismayed, eager, thrown, caught off guard.
  • Disgust: repelled, appalled, contemptuous, judgmental, uncomfortable, embarrassed, disapproving, nauseated, loathing, awkward, hesitant, aversion.
  • Calm: peaceful, relaxed, safe, settled, trusting, open, serene, at ease, accepting, loving, thoughtful, present.
  • Strength: confident, capable, respected, valued, courageous, determined, creative, free, energized, focused, appreciated, worthy.

No list is complete. If "wrung out" is the only phrase that fits, use it.

Every tool here is free and needs no account. Each walks you from a rough word to a precise one, asks where the feeling sits in your body, and offers a thought about what it might be asking for. The general one is The feelings wheel, about three minutes. The others start from a feeling you already half know:

  • Which kind of anxious, for narrowing a wide word to the flavor you are actually feeling.
  • Which anger is it?, because anger is not one feeling.
  • What is under the low, for a low patch that could be several things.
  • What is under the racing, for the feeling driving a fast mind.

Once you have the word, a short breath often helps it settle: The double-breath sigh for a feeling that has built up, The brake pedal breath for anger, A breath for a heavy chest for grief. The whole set lives under Emotions on the Discover page.

blocks.html: A feelings wheel helps you describe an emotion. It does not tell you whether that emotion is a symptom of anything, and Theraglee does not diagnose, screen for, assess for or treat any condition. If feelings are regularly bigger than you can handle, or are getting between you and your work, sleep or relationships, a licensed therapist can help, and the Theraglee directory lists license-verified clinicians. If you are in crisis, call or text 988 in the United States for the Suicide and Crisis Lifeline, or text HOME to 741741. If you are in danger, call 911.

pages.h1: Breathing exercises for anxiety, with the steps written out
pages.intro: When anxiety spikes, breathing is the one part of the stress response you can take hold of directly. You cannot decide to slow your heart, but you can decide to breathe out for six seconds, and the rest of the body tends to follow. These five patterns are the ones people reach for most. Each is written out below so you can do it from this page, and each has a free guided timer on Theraglee.

blocks.html:
Four equal sides: in, hold, out, hold. The holds give a racing mind a count to follow and stop the breath speeding up again between rounds.

  1. Sit or stand with your feet flat. Breathe out fully to start.
  2. Breathe in through your nose for a count of four.
  3. Hold for four.
  4. Breathe out through your mouth for four.
  5. Hold, lungs empty, for four.
  6. Repeat for four to six rounds, about two to three minutes.

When it fits: before something you are dreading, in a bathroom stall at work, in the car before you go in. It is steadying rather than sleepy, so it suits the middle of the day. If a four-count hold is too much, use three; the square only has to be even. The guided version is Box breathing, three minutes.

A short breath in, a long hold, and a longer breath out. Physician Andrew Weil popularized this pattern, and the long exhale is what people notice first: it makes the next inhale slower on its own.

  1. Rest the tip of your tongue behind your top front teeth and breathe out through your mouth with a soft whoosh.
  2. Close your mouth and breathe in quietly through your nose for four.
  3. Hold for seven.
  4. Breathe out through your mouth, with the whoosh, for eight.
  5. That is one round. Do four rounds to begin with.

When it fits: at the end of the day, in bed, or whenever the body will not wind down. The hold is long, so if you feel strained, shorten every number in the same proportion and keep the shape. The guided version is The 4-7-8 breath.

The simplest of the five, and for many people the most reliable. No holds, just an out-breath longer than the in-breath. A longer exhale is the part of breathing most closely tied to the body's settling response, which is why nearly every calming pattern lengthens it.

  1. Breathe in through your nose for four.
  2. Breathe out through your nose or softly pursed lips for six.
  3. Keep going for two to five minutes. Let the breath stay quiet rather than big.

When it fits: when you need something you can keep doing while you walk, talk or lie in the dark. Once six feels easy, try four in and eight out. The guided versions are Four in, six out for bedtime and The long exhale for the four-and-eight pattern.

blocks.h2: The physiological sigh (double inhale, long exhale)
blocks.html:
Two breaths in through the nose, the second a small top-up on the first, then one long slow breath out through the mouth. It is the shape of the sigh a body makes on its own after crying, and the name comes from neuroscientists who studied why that sigh settles people. The second inhale reopens the small air sacs in the lungs, so the exhale carries more out with it.

  1. Breathe in through your nose until your lungs feel fairly full.
  2. Without breathing out, take one more short sip of air through your nose.
  3. Breathe out slowly through your mouth until your lungs are empty, longer than both inhales together.
  4. One to three rounds is usually enough. It is not meant to be repeated for minutes.

When it fits: the fastest of the five, for a moment with no time to sit down: a wave of panic on a train, the second before you speak, the pause after a sharp message. The guided versions are The double breath, Two breaths in, one long breath out for a sprinting mind, and The double inhale for a busy workday.

Paced breathing is breathing at a slow, even pace, usually around five or six breaths a minute, and keeping it there. No holds, no tricks. The steadiness does the work, which makes it the easiest pattern to keep up for several minutes and the best one to practice when you are not anxious, so it is familiar when you are.

  1. Breathe in for five.
  2. Breathe out for five.
  3. Continue for three to five minutes. If your mind wanders, come back to the count without comment.

When it fits: a daily practice, a long wait, or a slow return after a hard hour. If counting feels like effort, hum the whole way out instead; the hum stretches the exhale for you. The guided versions are Coherent breathing at five and five, Count the breath, not the worry for a worried mind, The humming breath and Three breaths before the call for the minute before a meeting.

blocks.h2: A word on dizziness, and when to stop
blocks.html: Slow breathing should feel like less effort, not more. If you get light-headed, tingly or short of breath, you are probably breathing too deeply or holding too long: stop, breathe normally until it passes, then try again with smaller breaths and shorter counts. Never force a hold, and skip the holds if you are pregnant, have a heart or lung condition, or your doctor has told you to avoid breath-holding. Breathing exercises are a way to steady yourself in a moment, not a treatment for a condition, and Theraglee does not diagnose, screen for or treat anything. If anxiety is a regular visitor, a licensed therapist can help with more than breathing; the Theraglee directory lists license-verified clinicians. If you are in crisis, call or text 988 in the United States for the Suicide and Crisis Lifeline, or text HOME to 741741. If you are in danger, call 911.

faq.q: What is box breathing?
faq.a: Breathing in for four, holding for four, breathing out for four and holding for four, repeated for four to six rounds. The even holds give a racing mind a count to follow. It is steadying rather than sleepy, so it suits the middle of the day.

faq.q: How does the 4-7-8 breath work?
faq.a: You breathe in through the nose for four, hold for seven and breathe out through the mouth for eight, for about four rounds. The long exhale slows the next inhale on its own, which is why many people use it at bedtime.

faq.q: Which breathing exercise is best for anxiety?
faq.a: The one you will actually do. The extended exhale (in four, out six) is the simplest and easiest to keep going; the physiological sigh is the fastest when there is no time to sit down; box breathing suits a moment of dread before something.

faq.q: Is it normal to feel dizzy during breathing exercises?
faq.a: It happens when the breaths are too deep or the holds too long. Stop, breathe normally until it passes, and try again with smaller breaths and shorter counts. Skip the holds if you are pregnant or have a heart or lung condition.

pages.title: Grounding Techniques: Seven Ways Back Into the Room — Theraglee
pages.description: Seven grounding techniques with short how-tos: the 5-4-3-2-1 senses method, cold water, feet on the floor, naming categories, an anchor object and movement.
pages.h1: Grounding techniques: seven ways to come back into the room
pages.intro: Grounding is anything that pulls your attention out of a spiral and back to where your body actually is: this chair, this floor, this cold tap. It does not argue with the thoughts. It gives the senses something real to hold so the alarm can run down. These seven are the ones people use most, each with a short how-to you can follow from this page.

blocks.html:
The best-known grounding technique, and a good one to learn first because it needs nothing but the room you are in.

  1. Name five things you can see. Say them out loud or in your head, with detail: the chipped mug, the green exit sign.
  2. Name four things you can feel: the chair against your back, the fabric of your sleeve, your feet in your shoes.
  3. Name three things you can hear, including the quiet ones.
  4. Name two things you can smell, or two smells you like if the room has none.
  5. Name one thing you can taste, or take a sip of something.

Go slowly. The counting matters less than the noticing, and if you lose your place, start the number again. The guided version is Five senses grounding, about four minutes.

Sharp cold is hard to ignore, which is why it works when a spiral has gone past where words can reach. Run cold water over your wrists for thirty seconds, splash your face, hold an ice cube in your palm, or press a cold can against the back of your neck. Breathe out slowly while you do it. Warmth works too, in a different way: a hot shower or a mug held in both hands can settle a shaky body. Use whichever is available and stop if it becomes painful. The guided version is The cold water reset, a minute with the water and a few minutes after.

Sit or stand and put both feet flat. Press them down as if you were trying to leave footprints, and notice the floor pressing back. Feel the heel, the ball, each toe. Then let the pressing go and notice how much of your weight the ground is already carrying. Thirty seconds of this is often enough to feel the difference between a mind that has left the room and a body that never did. If sitting still makes it worse, walk instead, slower than feels natural, with your attention kept in the soles. A slow walk, felt from the feet is seven guided minutes of exactly that.

blocks.h2: 4. Naming categories, an anchor object, movement, and saying where you are
blocks.html:
Four more that are short enough to use anywhere.

  • Name objects or categories. Give the thinking mind a small, boring job so it stops running the alarm. Pick a category and list everything you can: dog breeds, cities that start with M, things in your kitchen that are blue. Or go around the room naming every object in a flat voice: lamp, book, cable, window. Keep it concrete and a little effortful; counting backward from one hundred by sevens does the same thing for people who like numbers.
  • Carry an anchor object. A smooth stone, a ring you can turn, a bit of textured fabric, a key with a worn edge. Keep it in a pocket and, when the spiral starts, hold it and describe it to yourself: its weight, its temperature, its edges. Choosing it on a calm day is part of what makes it work later.
  • Move. Anxiety is a body ready to run, so running a little often helps. Shake out your hands, roll your shoulders, do ten slow squats, climb a flight of stairs, or walk to the end of the block and back. Tensing every muscle for five seconds and letting go all at once works when you cannot leave your seat; Tense and release walks you through the whole body.
  • Say the date and place. Out loud if you can: "It is Tuesday, November 2nd. I am in my kitchen in Columbus. I am thirty-four. The thing I am afraid of is not happening in this room." It sounds too simple to help, and it helps, especially when a memory or a what-if has taken over.

blocks.h2: Choosing your own order, and the free tools
blocks.html:
Nobody's list works in the same order. One person needs the cold water before the senses method will stick; another needs to move first. It is worth deciding your order on a calm day, so you do not have to think when it is loud. Your grounding order has you rank these moves from most trusted to least, Signs your body is on alert helps you spot the early tells so you can start sooner, and Where you are right now, on six dials is a one-minute check before and after, so you can see what moved.

pages.h1: Mood tracker: one tap a day, and after a week you can see what moves with it
pages.intro: Most people can say how they feel today. Far fewer can say what their week looked like, or whether the bad days had anything in common. A mood tracker fixes that by asking the same few questions every day and lining up the answers. Theraglee's is free with a free account, and if you would rather not use an app at all, the paper version further down works too.

blocks.h2: What the Theraglee mood check-in asks
blocks.html:
The check-in sits on your dashboard's Today tab. It takes about a minute.

  • Today's mood. One tap on one of five faces, from the worst kind of day to the best. The tap saves straight away, so a day with only a face still counts as a day logged.
  • What might be shaping it. Nine factors, each rated 1 to 10 for how it feels today: factors like sleep, stress at home and at work, loneliness, physical activity and social contact. Every scale runs the same way, so a higher number is always the better day.
  • The weather, and how much it mattered. Pick the day's weather from a row of icons, then rate 1 to 10 how it affected you. Two people can have the same gray day and feel it very differently.

Press Submit and the day is done. Each day is final once submitted, so the record is an honest one, not one edited in hindsight.

For the first week the check-in just counts: how many days you have logged and how many are left. From the seventh day with a mood, in a row or not, it shows your patterns: which of the factors tend to move with your mood, in which direction, and whether the kind of weather does too. It also points at the factor that moves with your mood and has the most room to improve, as a place you might look first.

This is noticing, not scoring. There is no total, no grade and no threshold. The chart exists so you can see, for example, that your low days cluster after short nights or that loneliness tracks your mood more closely than you expected, and decide what to do with that yourself.

blocks.h2: An optional evening reminder, and who can see your log
blocks.html:
Under the faces is a box: Email me a reminder on days I have not checked in by evening. It is off until you tick it. If you turn it on, you get one short email in the evening on the days you have not yet submitted, and nothing on the days you have.

Your check-ins are private to your account. They are not shown to anyone else, and therapists do not see them, even if you switch on Theraglee Match Mode. You can download everything you have logged from your account page at any time.

  • New here: create a free account, and you will land on the check-in.

A good habit is to check in at the same moment each day, such as with your evening cup of tea or right after you brush your teeth. The reminder email is there for the days that moment slips.

blocks.h2: How to track your mood on paper
blocks.html:
If you want no app at all, a notebook does the job. Draw a table with one row per day and these columns:

  1. Date.
  2. Mood, 1 to 5. One is a very hard day, five is a very good one. Decide what each number means to you before you start and write the key on the first page, so a 3 in week one means the same as a 3 in week six.
  3. Two or three things you want to watch. Hours of sleep, stress, movement, time with people, alcohol, or whatever you suspect matters. Rate each 1 to 10 or write a number. Keep it to three columns or you will stop filling it in.
  4. Weather, in a word.
  5. One line of notes. What the day was mostly about, in your own shorthand.

Fill it in at the same time each day, and do not go back and change a day later. After two weeks, read down the mood column and look for the 1s and 2s. Then read across those rows. Patterns that would never occur to you in the moment are often plain on the page, and two weeks is usually enough to spot the first one.

pages.h1: How to get therapy clients: an honest guide for a private practice
pages.intro: Most advice on filling a caseload is either a sales pitch for one platform or a list of forty tactics you will never get to. This guide covers the handful of things that reliably bring clients to a private practice, roughly in the order they pay off, and says candidly where directories like Theraglee fit.

blocks.h2: Start by deciding who you are for
blocks.html:
The fastest way to get more clients is to be easier to choose. A prospective client comparing twelve listings is not looking for the most qualified therapist but for the one who seems to understand their particular problem. "I work with adults on anxiety, depression, relationships, trauma and life transitions" describes almost every therapist in the country, so it helps no one choose you.

Write one specialty line you can say out loud without wincing: who you work with, what they come in with, and if it fits, how you work. "I help new parents who feel like strangers in their own lives." "I see couples who are not sure whether to stay." You can still see other clients; the line is for the people reading, not a contract with yourself. If you do not have a niche yet, lead with the two kinds of clients you most enjoyed in training and revisit it in a year. A vague line never gets a chance to work.

blocks.h2: Answer the three questions every prospective client is asking
blocks.html:
A person deciding whether to contact you, on a directory or your website, wants to know three things, in this order:

  1. Can you help with what I have? Your specialty line, up top, in their words rather than yours. "Panic attacks" and "can't stop worrying" find more readers than "anxiety disorders."
  2. What would it be like to sit with you? A paragraph on how a session actually goes: your pace, homework or not, how the first appointment runs.
  3. How do I start? Your fee, which insurance you take or that you are private pay, whether you have openings now, and how to reach you.

Most profiles answer the third question badly. "Contact me to learn more" costs you clients who were ready to book but did not want to ask about money. Say the number.

A simple website of your own, even a single page, does the same job for people who find you by search or a friend's recommendation. It needs those three answers, your photo and a way to contact you that you check daily, not a blog. Our guide to writing a therapist bio goes through the wording.

blocks.h2: Directory listings: where they help and where they do not
blocks.html:
Directories work because they already have the traffic you do not. Someone types "therapist near me" and the directory, not your website, is what comes up. Psychology Today is the largest and the one most clients have heard of; TherapyDen is free; Zencare, GoodTherapy and Inclusive Therapists each serve a particular slice of clients; and Theraglee is a newer flat-rate directory where members who want a therapist to reach out can ask for that. Our guide to the directory landscape describes each one.

Three things are true at once: one or two listings done well bring more clients than five done carelessly; a listing is only as good as its first sentence and photo, because that is all a client sees in the results; and directories bring people who are comparing, so the fit has to be visible in seconds. Use the same specialty line everywhere, keep fees and openings current, and reply to every inquiry within a business day.

Be honest about the math. A $30-a-month listing that brings one new weekly client a year has paid for itself many times over; one that brings nothing in six months, after you have fixed the profile, is a listing to cancel. Our guide to what directories cost shows how to work that out.

blocks.h2: Build referral relationships in your town
blocks.html:
The most durable source of clients for most private practices is other professionals who meet the people you want to see before you do. Primary care physicians and pediatricians hear about sleep, panic and low mood every day; school counselors know which families are looking; clergy, attorneys, OB-GYNs and other therapists whose caseloads are full all send people somewhere.

Make it easy to refer to you. A referral source needs three things in one breath: who you take, whether you have openings, and how to send someone. "I have two evening openings for adults with panic and health anxiety, and they can text my office line" is a referral someone can make; "I do a bit of everything" is not. Say exactly that in a short letter, follow up with a conversation if you can get one, tell them when you have openings again, and thank them when a referral arrives, within what confidentiality allows. Colleagues who turn people away are the best referral partners you will have: ask them to send you the ones that fit your specialty, and send them the ones that fit theirs.

Being in network with insurers is the biggest lever on how quickly a caseload fills, and on how much you keep per session. Paneling fills faster, because most people search by insurance first and the client's cost is low; it comes with lower reimbursement, paperwork, credentialing delays that can run months, and less control over session frequency. Private pay keeps more per hour and keeps clinical decisions yours, but you have to find people who can afford it and compete on fit and reputation.

Many practices start paneled with one or two insurers to fill, then shift toward private pay as referrals build. Whichever you choose, state it plainly on every profile; it is the first filter clients apply. If you go private pay, a sliding scale with a stated range, or a few reduced-fee slots through a nonprofit like Open Path Collective, widens who can see you.

blocks.h2: Reviews and testimonials, within your ethics code
blocks.html:
For most local services, reviews are how strangers decide. Therapy is different. The APA Ethics Code and the ACA Code of Ethics both restrict soliciting testimonials from current therapy clients, and the ACA code extends that to former clients and anyone vulnerable to undue influence. Many state licensing boards have their own advertising rules, some stricter than the national codes. Check your board's before you do anything here.

What you generally can do: keep your Google Business Profile accurate, let colleagues who refer to you speak to your work, and never respond to a public review in a way that confirms someone was a client. What you should not do: ask a client for a review, offer anything in exchange for one, or quote a client without being certain your board permits it. A profile that answers the three questions well does more for you than a testimonial you should not have asked for.

No full practice was built by one clever move. It was a clear specialty, a profile that answered the right questions, two or three listings kept current, and referral relationships tended over years. The tactics that promise more, paid ads and social media schedules among them, mostly cost time better spent on a phone call to a pediatrician.

Set a small routine and keep it. Once a month: check that every profile shows the right fee, insurance and openings, reply to anything you missed, and write to one potential referral partner. Once a quarter: look at where your last few clients actually came from and move your effort toward those sources.

Theraglee is one of the directories on the list, not a replacement for the rest of this guide. blocks.h2: Why therapists look beyond Psychology Today
blocks.html:
Psychology Today is the largest therapist directory in the United States and the one with the most name recognition among clients. As of October 2026 it costs about $30 a month, and credentials on it are self-reported rather than checked against a licensing board. Prices change, so check its current page.

Therapists go looking for alternatives for a few recurring reasons. In large cities, the list of therapists for any search is long and a new profile sits far down it. Some want a directory that reaches a particular community, whether a cultural or identity group, people who need reduced fees, or people who want a vetted therapist rather than a long list. Some want to stop paying a flat fee for a listing that has gone quiet. And some want a directory where the client comes to them rather than the reverse. Headway and Alma are not directories in the traditional sense. They are platforms that credential you with insurers, handle billing and claims, and list you to clients searching within their systems. pages.h1: How to write a therapist bio that a prospective client actually reads
pages.intro: A therapist profile has one job: to let a stressed, skeptical person decide in about thirty seconds whether to contact you. Most bios are written for colleagues or the licensing board instead. This guide is how to write one for the person reading it, with example sentences and a checklist.

blocks.html:
Whatever directory or website it lives on, a bio that gets read has four parts, in this order.

  1. Who you help, and with what. One or two sentences, in the client's words. This is the only part most people will read, because it is all they see in search results.
  2. What working with you is like. A short paragraph on how sessions go: your pace, whether you give homework, how directive you are, what the first appointment looks like.
  3. Who you are. Your license, training and the experience that is relevant to the people in part one. Brief, and third for a reason.
  4. How to start. Fee or fee range, insurance you take or that you are private pay, whether you have openings, how to contact you and what happens next. If you offer a free consultation call, say so.

Aim for 250 to 400 words. Longer bios are not read more carefully; they are skimmed and abandoned.

blocks.h2: Three tests for your first sentence
blocks.html:
The first sentence does most of the work. Run it through three tests before you keep it.

  • The stranger test. Could a client who has never been to therapy understand it without looking anything up? "I use an integrative, psychodynamic and attachment-informed approach" fails. "I work with people whose relationships keep ending the same way" passes.
  • The mirror test. Does the reader see themselves in it? A sentence about you ("I am a licensed clinical social worker with fifteen years of experience") is not about them. A sentence about their situation is.
  • The swap test. Could you paste this sentence into another therapist's profile and have it fit? If so, it says nothing. "I offer a safe, nonjudgmental space" fits ten thousand profiles. Rewrite until it fits only yours.

blocks.h2: Write to one person, in specifics
blocks.html:
Picture the client you are best with and write to that one person. Writing to everyone produces lists ("anxiety, depression, trauma, grief, life transitions, self-esteem"), and lists are what every other profile has. Writing to one person produces sentences ("You have a good job, people think you have it together, and you lie awake most nights running through what you said in a meeting."). The second one loses some readers and wins the right ones completely.

Specifics do the same for the "who you are" section. A string of acronyms (LMFT, EMDR, CBT, DBT, IFS, EFT) reads as a wall. Pick the one or two that matter to your reader and say what they mean for them: "I'm trained in EMDR, which many of my clients choose because it does not require talking through every detail of what happened."

• Jargon. "Modalities," "psychoeducation," "holding space," "the therapeutic alliance." Say what you mean.
  • The phrases that are on every profile. "Safe space," "nonjudgmental," "meet you where you are," "journey." None of these are false. All of them are invisible.
  • Your full CV. Where you did your internship, every workshop, the thesis topic. Keep the two items relevant to the client in front of you.
  • Your reasons for becoming a therapist. A single sentence can be warm. A paragraph makes the bio about you.
  • Everything you treat. Pick the few things you are best at; the bio is for being chosen, not for being complete.
  • Anything a licensing board would question. Promises of outcomes, claims of being the best or the only, and testimonials you solicited. The APA and ACA ethics codes and most state boards have rules here; read yours.

Clients look at the photo before they read a word. A good one is recent, in focus, and shows your face at roughly the size it would appear across a room: head and shoulders, looking at the camera, a plain or softly blurred background, natural light rather than flash. Wear what you would wear to a session.

Avoid sunglasses, cropped group photos, a logo in place of a face, and the headshot that looks like it belongs in a corporate directory. A phone photo taken by a friend outdoors on an overcast day, with you looking like someone a client could talk to, beats most paid portraits. Use the same photo everywhere so people recognize you.

These are generic examples written for this guide, not quotes from any real profile.

Before: "I am a Licensed Professional Counselor with over a decade of experience treating anxiety, depression, trauma, relationship issues and life transitions using an eclectic, client-centered approach."
After: "If you are in your thirties, doing well by every outside measure, and quietly exhausted by how much effort it takes, I can help."

Before: "I provide a safe, nonjudgmental space where clients can explore their inner world."
After: "Sessions with me are conversational. I will ask a lot of questions in the first few meetings, and I will tell you what I am noticing rather than keep it to myself."

Before: "Modalities: CBT, DBT, EMDR, ACT, IFS, mindfulness-based interventions."
After: "I am trained in EMDR and CBT. With trauma, that means we can work on how a memory affects you now without you having to narrate it in detail."

Before: "Contact me today to begin your healing journey."
After: "I charge $160 a session and am not in network with insurance, though I can give you a receipt to submit. I have two weekday evening openings. Message me here and I will reply within one business day to set up a free fifteen-minute call."

• The first sentence passes the stranger, mirror and swap tests.
  • The reader can tell within two sentences whether you work with people like them.
  • There is a paragraph on what sessions are actually like.
  • Credentials are brief, and each one says what it means for the client.
  • Fee, insurance and current openings are stated, not hinted at.
  • There is a clear next step and a promise about how fast you reply.
  • No jargon, no phrases that fit every other profile, no promised outcomes.
  • Your photo is recent, looks like you, and is the same one everywhere.
  • The whole thing is under 400 words.
  • You have read it aloud once and cut what you stumbled over.

One difference is worth knowing when you write it: through Theraglee Match Mode, members who want a therapist to reach out appear on your dashboard, and when you message one, your public profile is what they open to decide whether to reply. The specialties, ages, insurance plans and locations you list also decide which members you see, so a clear, specific profile makes a match work in both directions. pages.h1: Private practice marketing: twelve ideas, ranked by effort and payoff
pages.intro: Marketing a therapy practice is mostly a matter of being easy to find, easy to understand and easy to refer to, then doing that consistently. Here are twelve ways to do it, ranked roughly from least effort to most, with an honest word on what each one tends to pay back. None of them involves fear-based ads or promising results, because those are both bad marketing and against most ethics codes.

blocks.html: Effort is how much time an idea takes to set up and keep going. Payoff is how many of the right clients it tends to bring, and how long that keeps happening after you stop pushing. The best ideas are low effort and high payoff, and most of those are near the top. The ones lower down take more sustained work but build something that compounds: a reputation with referrers, or a steady trickle from search. Pick two or three from the top, do them properly, and add from lower down only when those are running.

1. Track where clients come from. Low effort, and the idea that makes every other one on this list measurable. Ask every new client, on the intake form or the first call, how they found you, and write the answer in a spreadsheet with the date. In six months you will know which of the next eleven ideas are working for you. Keep the record free of anything clinical and store it as you would any client information.

2. A Google Business Profile. Low effort, high payoff for anyone with an office. It is free, it is what shows up on the map when someone searches "therapist near me," and most practices either have none or have one with the wrong hours. Fill in the address, hours, phone, website, a photo of the entrance and a description that uses your specialty line. Do not solicit reviews; see the ethics note below.

3. One directory, done well. Low to medium effort, high payoff. Choose one directory, build the profile properly (our guide to writing a therapist bio covers how), keep fee, insurance and openings current, and answer every inquiry within a business day. A second directory that reaches a different kind of client is reasonable; five is not. Our guide to the directories describes the options.

4. A specialty page on your website. Medium effort, high payoff over time. One page, written in plain language, about the one problem you most want to be known for: what it feels like from the inside, how you work with it, what a first session looks like, how to start. That page is what search engines show someone typing "therapist for panic attacks" and your town, and it works for years. Write one before you write a blog.

5. Consultation calls. Low effort per call, high conversion. A free fifteen-minute phone call lowers the stakes of reaching out, lets both of you check fit, and turns inquiries into first appointments far more reliably than email. Put the offer on every profile and on your website, keep the call to fit and logistics, and end it with a concrete next step.

6. A waitlist that stays warm. Low effort, medium payoff. When you are full, do not just say no; say "I expect an opening in about six weeks, may I keep your name?" Then keep a short list, tell people honestly where they stand, and check in once a month so they know they are not forgotten. Many will still be waiting when a slot opens; those who found someone else will remember that you were kind about it.

blocks.h2: Reach the people who refer (ideas 7 to 9)
blocks.html:
7. Referral letters. Medium effort, high payoff that builds slowly. Write to the physicians, pediatricians, school counselors, clergy, attorneys and fellow therapists in your area who meet your ideal client before you do. One page: who you work with, whether you have openings, how to send someone, and the number to call. Follow up with a call where you can, and tell them when you have openings again.

8. A monthly email to referrers. Medium ongoing effort, compounding payoff. Once a month, a few sentences to the people on your referral list: your current openings, one thing you have been working on, one useful resource. No marketing voice. The goal is that when a patient says "I can't sleep and I'm anxious all the time," your name is the one that comes to mind, because they heard from you last week.

9. A talk at a school, workplace or community group. High effort per event, medium to high payoff. A forty-minute talk on something practical, such as how to talk to teenagers about stress, puts you in a room with dozens of potential referrers and clients at once. Keep it educational, offer a handout with your contact details, and do not sell from the stage. The invitations to speak again are the real return.

blocks.h2: Longer games, and one subtraction (ideas 10 to 12)
blocks.html:
10. A free worksheet download. Medium effort, slow payoff. A genuinely useful one-page worksheet on your specialty, offered on your website with no email address required, gets shared by other therapists and found by search over months. Write it for a lay reader and put your name and website at the bottom.

11. Answering questions in therapist-adjacent communities. Steady effort, slow payoff. Local parenting groups, school forums and professional associations all have people asking how to find a therapist. Answer the question honestly, without pitching, and let your name and specialty do the work over time. Never give clinical advice to a stranger online, and read each community's rules before you post.

12. Saying no to channels that do not work. Low effort, high payoff, and the one most practices skip. Every quarter, look at your tracking spreadsheet from idea 1. Anything that has cost money or hours for six months and brought no one is finished: cancel the listing, drop the social media schedule, stop the ads. Marketing that works is mostly a matter of doing fewer things for longer.

All of this sits inside your license. Do not promise outcomes; "I will help you overcome anxiety" is a claim you cannot make. Do not use fear ("untreated anxiety destroys relationships") to drive inquiries. Do not solicit testimonials from current clients; the APA and ACA ethics codes restrict it, the ACA code extends that to former clients, and your state board may be stricter still. Do not disclose that anyone is a client, including in replies to public reviews. Keep any tracking you do free of clinical detail and secured like any other record. When in doubt, your board's advertising rules are the authority, not a marketing blog.

The membership is one flat rate, $29 a month or $290 a year, with no per-session or per-contact fees, every listing is license-verified before it goes live, and the dashboard shows the referral stats that feed idea 1: profile views, calls to your protected Theraglee number, messages, website clicks, shares and Match Mode matches. Theraglee Match Mode adds one more: members who have asked a therapist to reach out appear on your dashboard, pseudonymously and only when their needs fit your listing, and you write first. Founding therapists pay nothing until their first member match, then $20 a month locked in, for the first 150 spots through December 31, 2026. The full offer is on the page for therapists.

pages.h1: How much do therapist directories cost? A plain comparison
pages.intro: Directory fees look small on the page and different once you work out what they come to over a year, or over one client relationship. This is a plain guide to the three ways directories charge therapists, with the arithmetic shown, the figures we verified in October 2026, and a way to work out your own real cost per new client.

blocks.html:
Nearly every therapist directory charges in one of three ways.

  • A flat fee, monthly or yearly, for a listing. You pay the same whether it brings you one client or twenty.
  • A per-session fee on clients the platform brought you, usually for as long as you see them. It costs nothing until it works, then it keeps costing.
  • Nothing in money. Free listings, often run by nonprofits or funded in some other way, which cost you the time to build and maintain a profile.

Each is a fair deal for some therapists and a poor one for others. This page makes the comparison in numbers.

Other paid directories, such as GoodTherapy, Zencare and Inclusive Therapists, charge flat or sliding-scale listing fees we did not verify for this page, so we have not quoted them. A flat fee's great virtue is that the cost per client falls as the listing brings more clients. Its risk is paying for months when it brings nobody, which is why a quarterly look at your numbers matters.

blocks.h2: Per-session fees, and what they add up to
blocks.html:
Headway is free to join. As of October 2026 it charges $9.99 per session for clients found through Headway, for the whole client relationship, a fee it announced that month. Prices change; check its current terms.

A per-session fee is easy to underestimate because each one is small. Here is the arithmetic, as an illustration rather than a prediction about any particular practice:

  • A client seen weekly for six months is about 26 sessions. At $9.99 a session, that is about $260 for that one client.
  • A client seen weekly for a year is about 52 sessions, or about $519.
  • Three clients, each seen weekly for six months, come to about 78 sessions, or about $780.

Set against a flat fee of $290 to $490 a year, a per-session model is cheaper only while it brings you very few sessions, and more expensive as soon as it works. That is the trade: no risk up front, a share of the revenue afterward. For a therapist who also gets insurance credentialing and billing from the same platform, part of that fee pays for paperwork, which is a real service; count it honestly on both sides.

blocks.h2: Free listings, and what they cost in time
blocks.html:
A free directory listing is not free. Building a profile properly takes an evening. Keeping openings and fees current and answering inquiries within a business day takes an hour or two a month for as long as the listing is up. If your time is worth what you charge for a session, a maintained free listing costs you a session or two a year, which is still cheap. A free listing with a stale profile and a slow reply costs you the clients who looked and moved on.

TherapyDen is free to list on. Open Path Collective is a nonprofit where you offer reduced-fee slots rather than pay a fee. Both are described in our guide to the directories.

blocks.h2: How to work out your real cost per new client
blocks.html:
The number that matters is not the monthly fee but what each new client cost you, from each source, and only your own records can tell you. The method is simple.

  1. Ask every new client how they found you, and record it with the date.
  2. For each directory, add up what you paid over the period: flat fees, or per-session fees on the clients it brought.
  3. Divide by the number of new clients from that directory in the same period. That is your cost per new client.
  4. Compare it to what a client is worth to you: your fee times the average number of sessions a client stays.

Give a new listing six months before judging it, and fix the profile first if it is bringing nothing. After that, keep a directory whose cost per client is a small fraction of what a client brings in, and drop one that has brought no one in six months with a good profile.

Suppose you charge $150 a session and your clients stay, on average, about 20 sessions, so a new client is worth roughly $3,000 to the practice over the relationship.

  • A flat-fee listing at $290 a year brings four new clients in the year. Cost per client: about $73. Against $3,000 each, the listing paid for itself with the first client.
  • A flat-fee listing at $360 a year brings one new client. Cost per client: $360. Still well worth it, if the client stayed, and a sign to improve the profile.
  • A per-session platform at $9.99 a session brings four clients who each stay 20 sessions: 80 sessions, about $799. Cost per client: about $200. Also worth it, though the fee is far higher than the flat-fee listing for the same four clients, and it grows with every additional session.

Your own numbers will differ. The point is that all three can be good deals, and that you only find out which is best for you with real figures rather than monthly prices.
